description: We are the SQAA team, a multidisciplinary group of passionate and innovative individuals from diverse academic backgrounds, including aeronautical engineering, cybersecurity, business, and environmental engineering. Our strength lies in combining our unique expertise, perspectives, and skills to tackle complex challenges and develop innovative, sustainable, and impactful solutions.
summary:
UBAR is a GIS index and website that finds where on Earth space experts can best rehearse missions to the Moon and Mars. It starts with Oman, home of the Samail ophiolite and the AMADEE-18 Mars simulation. We scored every 90 m square of Oman (38 million cells) against real landing and science sites measured by NASA orbiters: Jezero crater from MOLA, the lunar south pole from LOLA. Ten criteria cover terrain, temperature swings, wind, dryness, ancient riverbeds, water-formed minerals mapped by EMIT from the ISS, and access. Expert AHP weights then combine them into four mission profiles: Moon base, Mars landing, Mars science and Mars sedimentary.
The method passes blind tests. A held-out Oman Drilling Project site ranks in Oman's top 15%. Utah's Mars Desert Research Station, scored with the same method and no tuning, ranks in the top 11%. For Jezero-type life science, Oman's ophiolite outscores Utah (0.78 vs 0.54). We flew a drone over one of the top-ranked sites to check the predictions on the ground. At ubar.space, anyone can pick a destination, set their own constraints and explore Oman's best Moon and Mars twins. The name honours Ubar, the lost Omani city NASA's space radar helped find in 1992.
details:
What it does. Space agencies rehearse Moon and Mars missions at "analog" sites on Earth. These are usually chosen by expert judgement and logistics, one site at a time. UBAR turns the choice into a measurable, repeatable map. For every 90 m cell of Oman, the Analog Suitability Index (ASI) says how closely that ground matches a specific Moon or Mars destination, for a specific mission.

How it works.

1.       Measure. Ten criterion maps cover all of Oman:

o        Terrain: slope, roughness (TRI) and local relief, from the Copernicus 90 m DEM.

o        Climate: day–night and yearly temperature swings, from MODIS land surface temperature; wind, from NASA POWER.

o        Dryness: plant cover, from MODIS NDVI.

o        Water history: ancient drainage channels.

o        Chemistry: water-formed minerals (serpentine, carbonates, Fe-Mg clays, sulfates), from EMIT L2B on the ISS.

o        Logistics: access, and distance from villages, farms and oil infrastructure (OpenStreetMap).

2.       Compare with real targets. Moon and Mars target values are measured from orbit at the real sites: LOLA at Shackleton crater on the lunar south pole, MOLA at Jezero crater (the Perseverance landing site). Terrain is compared at matched scale; Mars terrain is rebuilt at 450 m to match MOLA. Fuzzy similarity rules turn each Oman measurement into a 0–1 match.

3.       Weigh per mission. Hierarchical AHP weights are set for four profiles: Moon base, Mars landing, Mars science and Mars sedimentary. All consistency ratios are below 0.10.

4.       Score. ASI = Σ weight × match over 38 million cells, with hotspot maps of the top 10–20% and ranked candidate sites.

5.       Validate.

o        Oman Drilling Project sites: the surface-sample site ranks at the 97.5th percentile, and Wadi Lawayni, held out from tuning, at the 85.8th. AUC is 0.84.

o        Changing any weight by ±20% moves a site by at most 9 points.

o        External test: Utah's Mars Desert Research Station, scored blind with identical rules, ranks in Oman's top 11%.

o        AMADEE-18 (Dhofar) scores well for terrain but low for minerals: it looks like Mars but is not chemically like Mars, which the index separates.

6.       Field check. On 15 Nov 2026 we flew a DJI drone over candidate site S05 near Ibra (ranked #4 for Mars science): 0.47 km², about 1,400 photos, about 4 cm per pixel. We use the survey to compare satellite predictions with the ground and to build a 3D model for the website.

The website, ubar.space. A non-expert can:

•         pick a destination (Jezero, the lunar south pole and others) and stand on its real terrain in 3D;

•         "travel" to its closest Oman twin;

•         change the mission weights or add constraints (such as "stay 5 km from villages") and see the map update live, with a reality check showing whether known analogs still rank on top;

•         open a site passport explaining why a place scores and what Earth cannot copy (gravity, atmosphere, polar cold);

•         view sites in 3D and VR.

Benefits.

•         Mission and analog planners get an evidence-based shortlist per mission in minutes.

•         Oman gets a ready map for hosting future expeditions.

•         Students and the public see the Moon and Mars, and then the place in Oman that resembles them.

The method transfers to any country with the same global datasets.

Honest limits. Oman cannot reproduce gravity, a thin atmosphere or polar cold; its best Shackleton twin is only 32% alike, and the site says so. Mars terrain data is 463 m resolution. The drainage-channel layer has artefacts in dune fields. EMIT does not cover all of Oman, and gaps are flagged.

Tools and languages.

•         GIS and analysis: QGIS (PyQGIS, GDAL, SAGA), Python (rasterio, NumPy, Pillow).

•         Web: vanilla JavaScript (ES modules), MapLibre GL JS, three.js, HTML/CSS, hosted on AWS EC2.

•         Data access: NASA Earthdata, AppEEARS.

•         Field: DJI drone, DJI Terra photogrammetry.


Use of Artificial Intelligence

We used Claude (Anthropic) to help write code, analyse data, produce video and audio and draft text; all outputs were reviewed and run by the team, and no AI-generated images or NASA branding are used.
